questionStem: A 67-year-old white man comes to the physician because his wife is concerned about a freckle on the back of his neck. He says he has had the freckle for many years, but he has noticed that it has grown during the past 6 months. His brother died of liver cancer at the age of 50 years. Examination shows a 3-cm lesion at the base of the skull. A photograph of the lesion is shown . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: For melanoma, any biopsy technique other than a full-thickness biopsy is inappropriate, as depth of the lesion is important to determine (D, E). Given the danger of melanoma
incorrectExplanation: (A) watching or (B) applying topical therapy is also inappropriate.

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman has had intermittent fever, malaise, and a generalized rash for 2 weeks. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. There is a generalized erythematous maculopapular rash over the palms and soles. She has patchy alopecia of the scalp and eyebrows. Hematocrit is 36%, and leukocyte count is 9000/mm 3 (70% segmented neutrophils and 30% lymphocytes) . She is given intravenous aqueous penicillin G. Two hours later, she has severe chills, headache, tachycardia , flushing , and hyperventilation . Her temperature is 39.4 °C (103°F), and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acute condition?
correctExplanation: There is no clinical evidence to suggest this is toxic shock syndrome, which may initially present as a similar diffuse erythematous macular rash that includes involvement of the palms and soles, but it typically progresses to desquamation of the palms and soles one to two weeks later and is often accompanied by multiorgan system involvement. ,.

questionStem: A 53-year-old man notices a lump in his neck. Examination shows a hard 2-cm nodule in the lower left pole of the thyroid gland. Needle biopsy shows papillary carcinoma , and he undergoes total thyroidectomy . Five days later, he reports facial numbness and tingling , muscle pain, and hoarseness . Physical examination shows laryngeal stridor and a positive Chvostek sign. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.D: Administration of 50,000 U of vitamin D

correctExplanation: The patient is exhibiting signs of severe hypocalcemia, due to acute hypoparathyroidism, a known complication of thyroidectomy. Immediate treatment with intravenous calcium gluconate is warranted (B is correct). While the patient has evidence of stridor, he does not yet show signs of respiratory compromise, and treatment of the hypocalcemia should abate the laryngospasm, making endotracheal intubation at this time inappropriate
incorrectExplanation: (E is incorrect) . High dose vitamin D is often used in the chronic management of hypoparathyroidism but is not indicated in this emergency situation (D is incorrect). Corticosteroids may induce tetany in hypoparathyroid patients and would be inappropriate at this time (C is incorrect). Administration of 0.9% isotonic saline followed by diuresis would be appropriate in the management of hypercalcemia but would not be appropriate in this patient (A is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 77-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent mild abdominal pain. He also has had rectal pain with bowel movements and occasionally notices traces of red blood in his stool. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, benign prostatic hyperplasia , and hypertension . Current medications include insulin, tamsulosin , lisinopril , and hydrochlorothiazide ; verapamil was added 4 months ago. A colonoscopy performed 1 year ago showed no abnormalities . He is not in distress . His blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Examination shows moist mucous membranes . The abdomen is slightly distended and nontender. The prostate is enlarged, and there is an external hemorrhoid . Rectal examination shows hard stool in the rectal vault. Sensation to light touch and vibration is intact over the distal lower extremities. An x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple air-fluid levels and stool throughout the bowel. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
correctExplanation: With a presentation of abdominal pain, pain with bowel movements , intermittent hematochezia, and external hemorrhoids, constipation is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms. Dose-dependent constipation is a well-known side effect of verapamil and can be seen in up to 25% of patients, and given the timing of his symptoms after verapamil was started, it is the most likely cause (A is correct) . While colon cancer can cause abdominal discomfort, constipation, and hematochezia , a normal colonoscopy just one year ago makes this much less likely
incorrectExplanation: (B is incorrect). The presence of moist mucus membranes makes dehydration leading to constipation much less likely as well (C is incorrect). Diabetic neuropathy can lead to motility dysfunction in the GI tract but is more commonly associated with gastroesophageal reflux, gastroparesis, and chronic diarrhea ; this is also more likely amongst type 1 diabetics vs. type 2 diabetics (D is incorrect). The most common symptom at presentation of metastatic prostate cancer is bone pain; among other symptoms at presentation , urinary symptoms such as hematuria, inability to void or incontinence are much more likely than constipation (E is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of increasing confusion. She is left-hand dominant. Her medications are lisinopril and metformin. On admission , she is awake and alert. Her temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. correctExplanation: There is no suggestion of brain edema , so mannitol is not necessary.
incorrectExplanation: (D) There is no indication to provide heparin. (F) Pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is used to treat toxoplasmosis which may cause these symptoms but is more likely in patients that are immunocompromised which this patient is not. ,.

questionStem: A previously healthy 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of cough productive of white sputum. He has had no chest pain. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. His pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 136/86 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased throughout with a prolonged expiratory phase. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities . Spirometry shows an FEV 1: FVC ratio of 0.65. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.B: Diffuse infiltrative disease of the lung parenchyma
choices.E: Mass effect in peripheral lung parenchyma

correctExplanation: With chronic cough over 6 months, significant smoking history, and physical exam suggestive of hyperinflation and expiratory obstruction, the patient's history and exam are strongly suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/emphysema. The FEV 1:FVC ratio of less than 0.7 essentially confirms the diagnosis. The pathophysiology of emphysema is predominately that of alveolar destruction and fibrosis (A is correct). A diffuse infiltrative parenchymal lung disease such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or diffuse thickening of the pleura would most likely lead to a restrictive pattern on spirometry, with decreased FEV 1 and FEV, with a FEV 1:FVC ratio> 0.7 (Band Care incorrect). Histamine-mediated bronchospasm and edema is more likely to present as episodes of dyspnea and may be worsened by exercise or by certain triggers; cough may be present but is typically more common at night or in early morning
incorrectExplanation: (D is incorrect). A lung mass in the peripheral parenchyma of the lung is not likely to cause changes in spirometry; chronic cough may indeed be a symptom of lung mass but is more common with more central masses that affect the larger airways (E is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A previously healthy 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he was hit in his right flank by a hockey stick. He reports no blood in his urine. He rates his pain as a 6 on a 10-point scale. His pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation over the right flank. His hematocrit is 42%. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Spiral CT scan of the abdomen

correctExplanation: The patient presents with blunt trauma to the flank which may result in renal traumatic injury. In the absence of hematuria on urinalysis, the likelihood of renal trauma is low, and no further imaging or evaluation is required (E is correct). He is not showing any signs of hemodynamic instability or active bleeding, so urgent surgical intervention is not warranted
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). If hematuria were present, evaluation with CT scan of the abdomen would be warranted (D is incorrect). Retrograde urethrography would be indicated in the setting of suspected urethral injury in the setting of trauma to the penis, scrotum, perineum, or pelvis, which is not the case here (C is incorrect). Renal arteriography may be warranted in the setting of ongoing bleeding from renal trauma to allow for angioembolization; in the absence of hematuria, it is not warranted here (B is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 24-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fatigue. Menses occur at regular intervals with no excessive bleeding. She takes no medications or vitamin supplements. Examination shows no abnormalities except for pale conjunctivae . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dl. A blood smear is shown. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?
correctExplanation: A premenopausal woman with anemia who has regular menses and no other history of nutritional deficiencies would most likely have iron deficiency anemia caused from blood loss. Blood smear shows hypochromia and supports this diagnosis.
incorrectExplanation: (C) Niacin and (E) Be would not likely lead to anemia, and (A) folate and (D) B1 deficiencies have macrocytosis. ,.

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician 8 days after she had loss of consciousness while combing her hair. She says she felt light-headed before she passed out. During the past 3 months, she has had two similar episodes and has noticed that her left arm tires easily. She is left-handed . She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and atenolol. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years . Her pulse is 76/min and regular, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg in the right arm. Heart sounds are normal. The radial and brachia! pulses are absent on the left and present on the right. Pedal pulses are decreased bilaterally. Muscle strength and sensation are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: The "steal" comes from retrograde vertebral artery flow to aid blood flow to the affected arm, which leads to a loss of consciousness.
incorrectExplanation: (A) Coarctation of the aorta and (B) a cervical rib could cause the vascular symptoms of weakened pulses in the left arm, but typically would not lead to syncope and occur much earlier in life. (C) Raynaud disease is vasoocclusion of the small vessels and often has red, blue, and white skin discoloration, which is absent in this patient. (E) Thromboangiitis obliterans is certainly possible in this patient, but this disease affects medium to small vessels and the distribution of symptoms in this patient clearly are in large vessels. (F) A transient ischemic attack could explain the syncope, particularly in the vertebrobasilar system, but would not cause the peripheral symptoms. ,.

questionStem: A 35-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of dysuria and pelvic pain over the past 2 years. He is sexually active. Examination shows a tender prostate. Urinalysis shows 2-5 WBC/hpf . A urine culture is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: In this patient, the presentation of recurrent dysuria and tender prostate on exam is consistent with chronic prostatitis. While the most common etiologic agents are gram negative rods such as E. coli, a negative urine culture should prompt evaluation for Chlamydia trachomatis in sexually active men (B is correct). Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and causes painful genital ulcerations and does not cause symptoms of dysuria and urethritis
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). While primary infection with herpes simplex virus can cause dysuria, chronic, recurrent herpes simplex typically presents with small vesicular and ulcerative genital lesions (C is incorrect). Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, is associated with an ulcerative lesion (chancre) in early infection, which may progress to secondary and tertiary syphilis in chronic infection, which may present with systemic involvement of the cardiovascular or nervous systems (D is incorrect). Trichomonas vagina/is, while a rare cause of urethritis in men, can be identified in a high proportion of male sexual partners of infected women, though the infection is typically asymptomatic and self-limited (E is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of moderate numbness and weakness of his left hand. There is no history of trauma to the hand . He has hypertension treated with enalapril and type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin . He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m 2• His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Examination shows atrophy of the hypothenar muscles . The middle , ring, and small fingers are held in flexion ; there is weakness of abduction of the small finger. The patient cannot prevent paper from being pulled through his fingers. All other intrinsic hand muscles are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 1 + at the left brachioradialis, biceps , and triceps muscles . Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the palmar aspect of the left ring and small fingers and the hypothenar region of the hand. The remainder of the examination shows no other abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.C: Lesion of the lower trunk of the brachia! plexus
choices.D: Lesion of the medial cord of the brachia! plexus

incorrectExplanation: (A) Syringomyelia might cause similar symptoms but would typically affect both hands and cause deficits to temperature sensation. questionStem: A 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of light-headedness . She states that she feels as if she is going to pass out when she gets out of bed in the morning. She has not had chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations . She has hypertension and hypothyroidism . Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, enalapril, and levothyroxine . She appears fatigued . She is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m2• Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 64/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg while supine and 135/85 mm Hg while standing . Examination shows dry skin. The thyroid gland is symmetrically enlarged, nodular, and nontender. Jugular venous pulsations are present 3 cm above the sternal angle and decrease by 2 cm with inspiration. The lungs are clear to auscultation . A grade 1/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the left sternal border without radiation. There is trace pitting edema of the ankles. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Results of a complete blood count are within the reference range. Her serum potassium concentration is 3.4 mEq/L, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 1.5 µU/ml. choices.B: Serial measurements of serum creatine kinase activity

correctExplanation: An ambulatory ECG is needed to confirm bradycardia when she has her current symptoms, and the treatment would ultimately be a pacemaker.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman has decreased urine output 6 hours after admission to the hospital for treatment of a 3-day history of nausea and vomiting . She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy. Her outpatient medications were glipizide, atorvastatin , lisinopril, and 81-mg aspirin; all medications were held on admission . Her blood pressure was 82/40 mm Hg on admission . After beginning intravenous administration of fluids, her blood pressure increased to 110/70 mm Hg. On examination now, the abdomen is soft, and there is diffuse mild tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are decreased. There is decreased sensation to light touch over the feet. Laboratory studies show: On Admission Now Fingerstick blood glucose 4+ 4+ Serum Urea nitrogen (mg/dl) 38 54 Creatinine (mg/dl) 1.8 2.6 Urine Specific gravity 1.028 1.011 RBC (/hpf) 0-2 0-2 Casts None coarse granular Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's decreased urine output?
correctExplanation: The patient presented with hypotension and acute renal failure, which has since worsened and has developed coarse granular casts, suggesting acute tubular necrosis as a cause of her acute renal failure (C is correct). ATN is amongst the most common causes of AKI and is commonly due to hypotension. The fact that the patient's AKI did not improve with fluid resuscitation suggests ATN as the cause as opposed to prerenal azotemia. Acute glomerulonephritis is typically present with hematuria in the absence of a urinary tract infection; proteinuria may also be present
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). Acute interstitial nephritis typically presents with eosinophiluria, and urine sediment typically shows white cells, red cells, and white cell casts (B is incorrect). Bilateral hydronephrosis would typically present with hematuria or pyuria depending on cause of obstruction (D is incorrect). Rhabdomyolysis will typically present with dark red to brown urine, with elevated levels of urine myoglobin, and may have a small amount of RBC per high power field; casts are not typically seen (E is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever and cough with increasing production of purulent sputum for 24 hours. She has had asthma since childhood that is characterized by episodes of coughing and wheezing . Treatment with inhaled corticosteroids was begun 8 months ago. She has been hospitalized twice over the past 2 months for low-grade fever, increased sputum production , and a poorly resolving infiltrate in the left lower lobe; sputum cultures at that time grew normal flora and Aspergillus fumigatus . She is in moderate respiratory distress. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F) , pulse is 95/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Diffuse expiratory wheezes and crackles are heard at the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows a normal S 1 and S2 with no murmurs . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The presence of Aspergillus fumigatus on sputum culture, combined with uncontrolled asthma despite treatment with inhaled corticosteroids, and a fixed infiltrate on chest x-ray, makes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) the most likely diagnosis in this situation (A is correct). A positive skin test against aspergillus antigen and elevated lgE levels would be seen on lab testing. Bronchiectasis is commonly seen on CT scan. a1- Antitrypsin deficiency typically presents with emphysema and can also cause chronic liver disease, neither of which are present in this patient
incorrectExplanation: (B is incorrect). Cystic fibrosis may present with chronic, recurrent respiratory infections or symptoms of malabsorption; as this patient's symptoms are more subacute, cystic fibrosis is much less likely (C is incorrect). Pertussis typically presents as a chronic cough (without fever) after an initial 1-2 week period of mild cough, fever, malaise, and increased sputum production; radiographic infiltrates are not common, except in the case of secondary pneumonia (D is incorrect). Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) may present with cough, pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, and may be associated with renal involvement; a positive sputum culture makes the diagnosis of a vasculitic lung disease, such as Wegener, unlikely (E is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 77-year-old woman with osteoporosis and hypertension is admitted to the hospital because of progressive confusion during the past 5 days. Her husband reports that she has had constipation for the past week and abdominal pain for the past 3 days. She had right breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation therapy 2 years ago. Medications are alendronate , hydrochlorothiazide, and a calcium supplement containing vitamin D. She is alert. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F}, pulse is 78/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 156/82 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and tenderness throughout; there is no guarding or rebound. Rectal examination shows hard brown stool. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings . On mental status examination , she appears anxious and is not oriented to person , place, or time. Her serum calcium concentration is 14.8 mg/dl, and serum albumin concentration is 3 g/dl. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows multiple skull metastases. Which of the following is the strongest contributing factor for this patient's hypercalcemia?
correctExplanation: The patient has clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia with altered mental status and constipation, confirmed by elevated serum calcium. Of etiologies of hypercalcemia, malignancy is the most common, with breast cancer being the most common malignancy in the US. questionStem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood twice in the past hour. He appears robust and comfortable. His pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg while supine. There is mild epigastric tenderness. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Hematocrit is 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge him with instructions to return if the pain or vomiting recurs

correctExplanation: In the setting of significant hematemesis and tachycardia, the patient is in class 2 hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock, with a likely blood loss of 15-30% of their circulating volume. Volume resuscitation is the most appropriate next step with 0.9% saline (D is correct). Discharging the patient without appropriate evaluation would not be appropriate
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). A repeat hematocrit is not likely to change significantly at this time and would not change management (B is incorrect). Measurement of serum amylase would be helpful in the evaluation of pancreatitis; however, it would not be the next best step (C is incorrect). questionStem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased urine output over the past 48 hours. She has an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glipizide . She has no history of renal disease . Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), and respirations are 24/min . While supine, her pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. While sitting, her pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. She appears acutely ill and slightly lethargic . Examination shows decreased skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and flat neck veins. There is mild, generalized abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 15,000/mm 3 Serum Na+ c1- K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Urine Na+ pH Specific gravity Glucose Ketones 146 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 2.9 mEq/L 28 mEq/L 72 mg/dL 254 mg/dL 3.4 mg/dL 8 mEq/L 5.0 1.028 2+ trace Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Prerenal azotemia due to volume depletion

Her exam shows signs of dehydration with dry mucosa, decreased skin turgor, and intravascular volume depletion, evidenced by her orthostatic hypotension and tachycardia . If available , a urine creatinine would allow for the calculation of the fractional excretion of sodium, which, given the low urine sodium level, is likely to be quite low. With this clinical presentation, prerenal azotemia, one of the most common etiologies of acute kidney injury, is the most likely diagnosis (E is correct). Acute tubular necrosis can arise from a multitude of different clinical scenarios (most commonly ischemia from surgery, trauma , or sepsis), and its diagnosis is reserved until both prerenal and postrenal causes of acute kidney injury are ruled out (Bis incorrect). In the absence of physical signs and symptoms of urinary retention or hydronephrosis (readily seen on bedside renal ultrasound), obstructive uropathy is much less likely (C is incorrect). Postinfectious glomerulonephritis typically presents about 2 weeks after streptococcal throat infection or other bacterial or viral infections and is usually associated with significant proteinuria (D is incorrect) . ,. questionStem: A 62-year-old woman has had progressively severe midback pain over the past month. She has been fatigued and less mentally alert for 3 weeks. incorrectExplanation: (B) Mammography would be reasonable as a routine study but not to diagnose melanoma. (C) Bone scan is not typically done but could be considered if there is concern for marrow uptake or lytic lesions not seen on a skeletal survey but is not typically done. questionStem: Two days after a myocardial infarction, a previously asymptomatic 60-year-old woman develops pulmonary edema. A grade 4/6 systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Oxygen saturation in the right atrium and pulmonary artery is 65%, and pulmonary artery diastolic pressure is 35 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Torn chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve

correctExplanation: A ruptured interventricular septum might produce similar symptoms, but oxygenated blood from the left ventricle would enter the right and would make the oxygen saturation higher.
incorrectExplanation: (B) A ruptured left ventricular free wall would cause shock but not likely pulmonary edema and right-sided pressures would likely be lower. (D) A ruptured pulmonary valve would cause a diastolic murmur and would not lead to elevated pulmonary artery pressures. (E) A ruptured tricuspid valve would typically be heard on the sternal border compared to the apex and also would tend to have elevated vena caval pressure and lower pulmonary artery pressure. ,.

questionStem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was found unconscious on the floor of his apartment next to an open bottle of barbiturates . On arrival, his pulse is 118/min, respirations are 6/min, and blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Examination shows diffuse movement to painful stimuli. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ c1- K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Creatinine Creatine kinase Urine 140 mEq/L 106 mEq/L 6.1 mEq/L 14 mEq/L 27 mg/dl 5.7 mg/dl 10,000 U/L pH 6 Specific gravity 1.010 Blood positive Glucose negative Protein trace RBC 3-4/hpf WBC 0-2/hpf Pigmented granular casts4-5/lpf Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's renal failure?
correctExplanation: This all suggests rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of muscle and is characterized by a high serum potassium concentration and myoglobin present in urine (which activates the blood assay in a urine dipstick, but results in a negative erythrocyte count in urinalysis).
incorrectExplanation: (A) Glomerulonephritis would have evidence of nephritis with either erythrocytes or erythrocyte casts in the urine which is not present. (B) Acute interstitial nephritis is typically an allergic reaction to a drug, which is possible in this case, but would be manifested by leukocytes, leukocyte casts, and eosinophils present on urinalysis. (C) Bladder obstruction would typically have more azotemia and would be improved by removing the obstruction by placing a catheter, if possible. There is no evidence to suggest obstruction in this vignette, however. (D) Cholesterol emboli are usually released from atherosclerotic plaques during an invasive procedure such as angioplasty and are typically diagnosed by biopsy. This would be unlikely given the vignette. ,. "' , ~ r-- ,.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been amenorrheic for 3 months. She has also had increased facial hair growth and multiple episodes of acne over the past year; she has had a 27-kg (60-lb) weight gain during this time despite no change in appetite . Menses had occurred at regular intervals until 1 year ago, when they became increasingly irregular . She is not sexually active. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 36 kg/m 2• Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. Examination shows truncal obesity with pink striae. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Urine 13-hCG test is negative . Measurement of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Urine free cortisol concentration in a 24-hour specimen

correctExplanation: The patient has secondary amenorrhea and pregnancy has been ruled out. The fairly recent onset and fast progression of weight gain and hirsutism, along with violaceous striae in the absence of exogenous corticosteroids should raise suspicion for Cushing syndrome . First-line testing for Cushing syndrome should include measurement of a 24-hour urine free cortisol concentration (E is correct). This clinical picture also raises concern for hyperandrogenism, which may be a sign of an androgen-secreting tumor which would lead to elevated serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration; however, this condition is more common in post­ menopausal females
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). Measurement of estradiol and progesterone would be warranted in the evaluation of amenorrhea; however, the clinical features of hypercortisolism makes Cushing syndrome more likely and these would not be the first line of testing (B and Care incorrect). Urine catecholamines are elevated in pheochromocytoma, which commonly presents with hypertension, but is not associated with amenorrhea, weight gain, or hirsutism (D is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of increasing pain and redness of his left knee. (C) A Baker cyst is located in the popliteal fossa, and (E) Osgood-Schlatter disease (osteochondritis of the tibial tubercle) typically presents in adolescents or young adults as an anterior knee pain that increases gradually over time and is typically not associated with swelling or erythema. ,. questionStem: A previously healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an itchy rash on her face, arms, and hands for 2 days. She notes that the rash appeared 2 days after working in her garden. Examination shows urticaria! and vesicular lesions over the face, upper extremities , and hands. Which of the following is the most likely pathologic process of this patient's rash?

choices.A: Chemotaxis of eosinophils caused by direct antibody reaction with plant sap
choices.B: Destruction of adhesion among epidermal cells caused by circulating lgG autoantibodies directed against the cell

questionStem: A 62-year-old man with severe obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic disabling dyspnea . His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. He is plethoric, and jugular veins are distended . Breath sounds are distant, and the second component of S2 is accentuated. His FEV 1 is 0.5 L. incorrectExplanation: (D is incorrect), nor has severity of obstruction or elevated residual volume (B and C are incorrect). questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain of the fingers over the past 6 months. She has a 6-year history of cold sensitivity of the hands. On cold exposure , her fingers become initially pale and then turn blue; there is redness with recovery. She has a 3-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease . Examination shows tightening of the skin of the fingers, with erythema , scaling, and telangiectasias . Dry crepitant crackles are heard at both lung bases. X-rays of the hands show loss of tufts of some distal phalanges and scattered soft tissue calcifications . Serum antinuclear antibody testing is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.C: Positive findings for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and negative findings for antinuclear antibody
choices.D: Positive findings for antiribonuclear protein antibody

correctExplanation: The patient has symptoms of systemic sclerosis, particularly Reynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasis, and likely systemic sclerosis. Serology in this patient will typically show positive anticentromere antibody (B is correct); antinuclear antibody (ANA) is also typically positive; and anti-Scl-70 antibody is usually positive in patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. It is not likely that serologies would be negative in this patient
incorrectExplanation: (A is incorrect). Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody may be elevated in patients with vasculitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis , microscopic polyangiitis , or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (C is incorrect). Antiribonuclear protein antibody is typically positive in patients with mixed connective tissue disease, with overlap of symptoms of lupus, systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome , polymyositis , and dermatomyositis; patients typically present with fatigue, low grade fevers, myalgias, and arthralgias . Given that the patient has symptoms more consistent with systemic sclerosis alone, RNP is not likely to be elevated at this time (D is incorrect). Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are typically positive in systemic lupus erythematosus, which typically presents with fatigue, fevers, arthritis, and a typical erythematous rash in malar distribution or "butterfly rash." Photosensitivity is also common. (E is incorrect). ,. "' , ~ r-- r ,,, Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of the recent onset of shortness of breath. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 25 years. He is emaciated and in moderate respiratory distress . There is dullness to percussion and egophony at the right lung base. He has a leukocyte count of 18,200/mm 3 (60% neutrophils, 17% band forms , 20% lymphocytes , and 3% monocytes). An x-ray of the chest shows a right lower lobe infiltrate with a pleural effusion . Thoracentesis shows purulent, foul-smelling fluid . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: (A) is the correct answer in this scenario. The acute onset of shortness of breath, accompanying right lower lobe infiltrate and leukocytosis make an infectious etiology of his pleural effusion more likely. The presence of purulent fluid is diagnostic of empyema. While pneumococcal empyema (option D) is one of the most common causes of community-acquired pneumonia , the foul-smelling nature of the fluid, combined with the location of the pneumonia in the right lower lobe make aspiration pneumonia from an anaerobic organism more likely (D is incorrect). Tuberculous empyema is uncommon, especially in absence of risk factors for tuberculosis, and is usually seen when a cavitary lesion (typically located in the upper lobes) ruptures into the pleural space, causing a hydropneumothorax (E is incorrect). Malignant effusions typically present with slowly progressive shortness of breath, and are typically serous or serosanguinous on thoracentesis (C is incorrect). Chylothorax typically yields a milky fluid on thoracentesis and is usually associated with trauma or tumors of the mediastinum, neither of which are present in this patient (B is incorrect). ,. questionStem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of pneumonia . He has a 3-day history of fever, cough productive of greenish sputum , and mild shortness of breath. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease . Current medications include 81-mg aspirin, atenolol, isosorbide , glipizide, metformin , and rosiglitazone . He appears ill and has mild shortness of breath . His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 195/64 mm Hg. Moist crackles are heard at the left lung base. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 16,700/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 90% Ban~ 2% Lymphocytes 8% Serum Na+ K+ c1- Hco3- Glucose Creatinine AST ALT 137 mEq/L 4.8 mEq/L 97 mEq/L 20 mEq/L 180 mg/dL 1.5 mg/dL 18 U/L 12 U/L An x-ray of the chest confirms left lower lobe pneumonia . Immediate discontinuation of which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
correctExplanation: Aspirin Atenolol Glipizide lsosorbide Metformin Rosiglitazone The patient has pneumonia with elevated creatinine indicating acute kidney injury. Metformin is mostly excreted by the kidney, and, in the setting of renal impairment, will accumulate increasing the risk of potentially fatal lactic acidosis. Therefore, metformin should be discontinued at this time (E is correct). Given that the patient is hypertensive, it would be inappropriate to discontinue atenolol or isosorbide at this time (B and D are incorrect); in fact, he may require more antihypertensive therapy in this setting. Glipizide and rosiglitazone may be continued at this time for blood glucose control; however, his blood sugars should be monitored closely to ensure the patient doesn't develop significant hypoglycemia and rosiglitazone is no longer indicated for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus because of cardiovascular risk (C and F are incorrect). There is not an acute indication to discontinue aspirin at this time

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the emergency department because of an uncontrollable nosebleed for 6 hours. This is her fourth nosebleed over the past 2 weeks . questionStem: A 77-year-old man is brought by his wife for a follow-up examination 3 weeks after an episode of right middle lobe pneumonia. The pneumonia is improving with antibiotic therapy. Three months ago, he had a similar episode . His wife says that he swallows his food well, but he has had a slight increase in his chronic cough after meals. He has multi-infarct (vascular) dementia. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years, but he quit 15 years ago. He has never had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease . questionStem: A healthy 39-year-old man of German descent comes for a routine examination . He had a cholecystectomy at the age of 25 years. He has had several episodes of mild jaundice over the past 10 years that resolved spontaneously . He appears healthy . Examination shows no abnormalities except for splenomegaly . His hematocrit is 39%, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is 36% Hb/cell, and mean corpuscular volume is 80 µm 3. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative . A blood smear shows erythrocytes with loss of central pallor. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?

choices.D: Decreased erythropoietin concentration I} Pyruvate kinase deficiency

correctExplanation: There is no evidence of any autoimmune disease, and the negative result of the Coombs test makes autoimmune conditions unlikely.
incorrectExplanation: (C) The patient is in his 30s and takes no supplemental folic acid so a history of congenital dihydrofolate reductase deficiency is not likely. (D) There is no evidence of decreased erythropoietin concentration, and the patient has no known risk factors such as chronic kidney disease. (E) There is no reason to think the patient is deficient in folate or (J) vitamin B12 (cobalamin) because there is no evidence of macrocytosis. (G) Glucose 6- phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is unlikely in patients of northern European descent and would manifest after taking a substance known to stress the oxidative-reduction system (such as sulfa antibiotics) . (F) Globin chain mutations would result in smaller cells , typically a more profound anemia and auto-splenectomy at this age (rather than splenomegaly). (H) Lead poisoning is not likely given the information in the vignette, and (I) while pyruvate kinase deficiency certainly fits the clinical picture, it usually is more problematic in childhood and requires transfusions if the phenotype is significant. Neither has been included in the vignette, making spherocytosis more likely. ,.

questionStem: A 4 7-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive swelling of both legs and generalized weakness . He says he now has some difficulty performing his usual activities . Last year, he received the diagnosis of hepatitis B and C. He has a long-standing history of intravenous drug use.
